system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 30-year-old woman with a history of endometriosis, bipolar disorder, and recent pneumonia was readmitted with right-sided pleuritic chest and back pain, diarrhea, and headache. She had recently completed a course of levofloxacin, which she discontinued due to gastrointestinal side effects. Imaging revealed no pulmonary embolism or active infection; the pain was attributed to musculoskeletal or post-viral causes. Diarrhea resolved spontaneously and was likely antibiotic-associated. Hyperglycemia was noted, with A1C pending. Anxiety related to recent mania and current symptoms improved with continued psychiatric medications. She was discharged home with tramadol for pain, instructions to follow up on mental health and glucose issues, and advised to monitor for worsening symptoms.
problems: Unspecified antibiotic causing adverse effects in therapeutic use
Migraine, unspecified, without mention of intractable migraine without mention of status migrainosus

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I know you just got here and might still be feeling groggy. You were brought in after being found unresponsive in your car. Do you remember what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I… I took some of my meds. Clonidine, Haldol, and Zyprexa. I just felt so overwhelmed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for telling me. That’s important. You were very sleepy when EMS arrived—your breathing slowed down, so they had to put a breathing tube in to help you. You’re off the ventilator now and doing much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t remember that. Was I… intubated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, just for a short time. It was for your safety because you weren’t breathing well. The tube was removed yesterday afternoon. You’re breathing on your own now and that’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry. I didn’t mean to scare anyone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re just glad you’re safe. Your family said you’ve been doing better since your last hospitalization, but you were feeling more tired lately?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah. I thought it was just stress. And I looked up how much Zyprexa would… you know. I didn’t think I’d end up here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve checked your labs and scans. Your brain CT was normal—no bleeding or stroke. Your chest X-ray showed the breathing tube was a bit too far in at first, so it was adjusted. Your lungs are clearing now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was I in danger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were at risk because of the overdose. The medicines you took can slow your heart and breathing. Your GCS was low—8 out of 15—so we needed to protect your airway.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: GCS?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a scale we use to check alertness—eye opening, speaking, moving. 15 is fully awake, 8 means very drowsy. You’re back to normal now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also noticed your heart rhythm had a long QT interval—over 500 milliseconds. That can be dangerous and was likely from the overdose, especially the antipsychotics and clonidine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my heart okay now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We stopped the QT-prolonging meds for now, gave you fluids, and corrected your electrolytes. Your rhythm has improved and is back to normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know those could affect my heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not common at normal doses, but overdoses can cause serious effects. We’re monitoring you closely. Your blood work also showed a mild acid buildup—lactate was 3.0—but that’s resolved with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So everything’s getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your mental status has cleared, your breathing is stable, and your heart rhythm is normal. The main concern now is your bipolar disorder and safety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on lithium for years. I didn’t take extra of that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your lithium level—it was normal. The psychiatry team reviewed your case and wants you to continue it. It’s helping, and stopping could make things worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just feel so stuck sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. That’s why we’re arranging for you to go to a psychiatric facility after here. You’ll get more support and therapy to help manage these feelings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that like a lock-down place?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a safe place with 24/7 mental health care. You’ll have therapy, medication management, and support. It’s not punishment—it’s treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I guess I need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m checking in. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little sore throat from the tube, but otherwise okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. We can give you lozenges or ibuprofen for that. Your repeat chest X-ray shows your lungs are improving—no pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also tested for MRSA and C. diff—both negative. No infections. And your IV site is a little red—phlebitis—but it’s mild. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not unless it gets worse. For now, we’ll just monitor it and maybe switch the IV site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your telemetry shows your heart rhythm is stable. No more long QT. We’re going to discharge your lithium dose to 600 mg at bedtime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why the change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a bit higher, but the psychiatry team thinks it will help with mood stability. We’ll check your levels regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll take it as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made good progress. You’re alert, walking, eating well. The plan is to transfer you tomorrow to the psychiatric facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely normal. It’s a big step, but it’s for your long-term health. They’ll work with you on coping strategies and support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to see my family?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they can visit. And you’ll have phone access. It’s not isolation—it’s structured care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final update: all your labs are normal, your heart is fine, and you’re medically cleared. The transfer is set for tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You’re strong for getting through this. Keep working with the team, and things can get better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we ask. Your discharge meds include lithium, trazodone for sleep, albuterol if you wheeze, and iron for your B12 deficiency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep up with them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. And if you ever feel unsafe again, please reach out—call your doctor, go to the ER, or call a crisis line. You’re not alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to go through this again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a powerful step. We believe in your recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team is here. Just a few final words: you’re medically stable, and the psychiatric team is expecting you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve come a long way in five days. Keep going. We’ll send your records and care plan with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. And remember—help is always available.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll remember.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing the right thing by getting help. Wishing you strength and healing.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 30-year-old woman with bipolar disorder, asthma, and a history of multiple suicide attempts was admitted after being found unresponsive in her car following a drug overdose involving clonidine, haloperidol, and olanzapine. She presented with a GCS of 8, bradycardia, and respiratory depression requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation. Initial labs showed an elevated lactate and anion gap metabolic acidosis, both of which resolved with fluid resuscitation. CT head showed no acute intracranial abnormalities. She developed a prolonged QT interval, likely due to the overdose and bradycardia, which improved with supportive care and electrolyte repletion. She was extubated without complications and regained full mental clarity. Phlebitis at an IV site was noted but remained mild. Psychiatry recommended continuation of lithium therapy. She was medically stabilized and transferred to a psychiatric facility for ongoing care.
